items.e: It is the same whether one touches the tent [covering a corpse], or erects [the tent], or moves [the tent]: All of them are counted [as having been defiled through contact] with a corpse. Only a person can defile by carrying a corpse. Food and drink and vessels do not defile by being carried by (i.e., supported by the body of) a corpse. Said Rabbi Yosei, in the same way, you could say, "Anything that is defiled for seven days by a corpse is [only] defiled until the evening by a zav, [and] anything that is defiled until the evening by corpse is completely pure by a zav." How so? [If] one person [touches] another person, there are two [degrees of impurity] by a corpse * , and one [degree of impurity] by a zav. A vessel [that touches] another vessel: Three by a corpse and two by a zav. A vessel [that touches] a person [who touches] another vessel: Four by a corpse and three by a zav. When do these words apply? In regards to terumah and consecrated foods, but a nazirite only shaves [when he is defiled] by a corpse. And they are only liable for [causing] impurity to the Temple and its consecrated items on account of a corpse. Said Rabbi Akiva, I have a fifth [degree of impurity]: The tent-peg affixed to the tent (Mishnah Oholot 1:3). They said to him, the tent and the tent-peg are one and the same.

An idolater, and an animal, and an eight year-old, and an earthenware vessel, and food * , and liquids, [any of] which touch a corpse: Vessels that touch them are pure. And just as a limb of a corpse, or a limb [severed] from a living person that lacks the minimum quantity of bone is pure in regards to a human, so too with carrion and with sheratzim , [such a limb] is pure. A limb that does not have the appropriate amount of flesh on it (Mishnah Oholot 1:8): In regards to a human, it is impure; in regards to carrion and sheratzim , it is impure. The brain, whether of a human, a domesticated animal, a wild animal, fowl, carrion, tereifot , detestable things (i.e., insects), or creeping things: It is impure, and they are liable on account of it for piggul [and] notar , and it is impure and defiles with an olive's-bulk in regards to carrying, and with a lentil's-bulk in regards to touching. The general rule of the matter: The brain, behold, is like flesh in every respect.

[There are] nine [limbs] in the head, and the jaw is among them. Five in the knee, two on above and two below, and the protuberance in the middle. Anything that has tendons and bones, behold, that is a limb, and anything that does not have tendons and bones is not a limb. And one with extra [limbs] causes the count to rise. One missing [limbs], who only has two hundred, and one with extra [limbs], who has two hundred eighty: All of them join together for [the purpose of reaching the threshold of] one hundred twenty-five (see Mishnah Oholot 2:1). * One who is [still] alive: Neither [the principle of] "the majority of the [skeletal] structure" nor that of "the majority of the bones" apply.

A Jew who slaughtered an impure animal for a Gentile, [and] he slaughtered it [by cutting] two (i.e., the two simanim , the trachea and esophagus), or the majority of two, and [the animal] is still twitching, it defiles with the impurity of food, but not with the impurity of carrion. A limb that is separated from it is like one that separates from the living (i.e., a live animal), and flesh that separates from it is like [flesh] that separates from the living, and it is forbidden to Noachides, and even if the animal dies. [If it was killed] by stabbing, it [only] defiles with the impurity of food. [If] he slaughtered it with something that rendered it a tereifa , it has no impurity whatsoever. And a Gentile who slaughtered a pure animal for a Jew, and slaughtered it [by cutting] two or the majority of two, and it is still twitching, it defiles with the impurity of food but not with the impurity of carrion. And a limb that separates from it is like one that separates from the living, and flesh that separates from it is like [flesh] that separates from the living, and it is forbidden to Noachides, and even if the animal dies. [If it was killed] by stabbing, it defiles with the impurity of food. [If] he slaughtered [only] one [ siman ], or the majority of one, it has no impurity whatsoever. [If] he slaughtered it with something that does not render it a tereifa , and a Jew came and completed [the slaughter], it is permitted to eat. [If] a Jew slaughtered two or the majority of two with [something that does not render the animal a tereifa ], it is the same for both the Gentile and the Jew: He may cut flesh from it, and wait until it dies, and [the cut flesh] is permitted for eating.

The "ladleful of corpse-mold" that they spoke of (Mishnah Oholot 2:1) exists from the finger-joints and upwards, the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say, from the hollow of his hand. And what is a corpse that has corpse-mold? One who is buried naked in a stone coffin on top of the floor, or on top of a marble slab, but one who is buried with his clothing and in a wooden coffin on top of dirt does not have corpse-mold. And they remove dirt from under him, and that is "dirt of the graves," a ladleful and [a little] more (ibid.). Mixed blood * that is found in a grave but it is unknown what kind [of blood] it is: That is "dirt of the graves," a ladleful and [a little] more. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Tzadok explained, you separate the pebbles and the wood chips, and you remove that which is certainly [not dirt of the grave], and you leave that which is doubtful, and that is "dirt of the graves," a ladleful and [a little] more.

A spinal column, the majority of whose vertebrae were sawed off: Even though the structure [of the spine] remains intact, it is pure. [But] whenever it is inside a grave, even if it is broken, and even if it is crushed, it is impure, because the grave joins it together [with other sources of impurity].

A skull that has a long puncture-wound, or that had many puncture-wounds: They combine together [to constitute] the size of a drill hole. Said Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam, it so happened that in Ein Bul, there was one whose skull had [a piece] broken off, and the doctor brought him a patch made of a pumpkin shell, and he survived. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said to him, that is no proof. Even though he survived all the days of that year, once there was a rainfall, he caught cold on it (i.e., the patched skull), and he died.

An olive's bulk of flesh that separates from a limb of the living (i.e., a living person): Rabbi Eliezer says, it transmits impurity. They came back to Rabbi Eliezer with three (alt., "two" (GR"A)) responses. "No. If you are comparing this situation to a corpse * that [transmits impurity if it] possesses the greater part of a quarter-kav of corpse-mold * , can you say the same regarding a limb of the living, which does not [transmit impurity if it] possesses [the greater part of] a quarter-kav of corpse-mold?" Another matter: "Who dangles from whom? Does the limb of the living dangle from the flesh, or does the flesh dangle from the limb? The flesh dangles from the limb! Can it be possible that the flesh would transmit impurity by touch and by carrying and by [being under] a tent, while the limb [itself] remains pure?" Said Rabbi Shimon: "I would be astonished if Rabbi Eliezer [really did] render [an olive's bulk of flesh from the limb of the living] impure. Rather, he did not render it impure except in a situation where the limb possesses a sufficient quantity of flesh, such that both this and that (i.e., the limb and the flesh) may transmit impurity by touch and carrying and by [being under] a tent.

A bone the size of a barleycorn that separates from a limb of the living: Rabbi Nechunia renders it impure. They came back to Rabbi Nechunia with three (alt., "two" (GR"A)) responses. "No. If you are comparing this situation to a corpse that [transmits impurity if it] possesses [the greater part of] a quarter-kav of corpse-mold, can you say the same regarding a limb of the living, which does not [transmit impurity if it] possesses [the greater part of] a quarter-kav of corpse-mold?" Another matter: "Who dangles from whom? Does the limb of the living dangle from the flesh, or does the flesh dangle from the limb? The flesh dangles from the limb! Can it be possible that the flesh would transmit impurity by touch and by carrying and by [being under] a tent, while the limb [itself] remains pure?" Said Rabbi Shimon: "I would be astonished if Rabbi Nechunia [really did] render [a bone the size of a barleycorn that separates from the limb of the living] impure. Rather, he did not render it impure except in a situation where the limb [itself] possesses a bone the size of a barleycorn, such that both this and that (i.e., the limb and the flesh) may transmit impurity by touch and carrying and by [being under] a tent. Rabbi Yehoshua responded to the words of both of them: "Just as just as the living has 248 limbs, bone and flesh that separate from it are pure, does it not follow that [in regards to] a limb, which does not contain 248 [limbs within it], that the bone and flesh and separate from it should be pure?" Rebbi responded to the words of Rabbi Yehoshua: "No. If you hold that in regards to [bones and flesh that] separate from the living, that they certainly separated from something that is pure, can you say the same as to that which separates from a limb [of the living], which certainly separated from something that is impure?"

Said Rabbi Yehuda: Rabbi Akiva and the Sages did not disagree about a quarter- log of blood that separated from two corpses, that it is pure. About what did they disagree? About a quarter- log of blood that separated from two quarter- logs from two corpses, for Rabbi Akiva renders it impure and the Sages render it pure. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Akiva and the Sages did not disagree about a quarter- log of blood that separated from two quarter- logs from two corpses, that is is impure. About what did they disagree? About a quarter- log of blood that separated from two corpses, for Rabbi Akiva renders it impure and the Sages render it pure (see Mishnah Oholot 2:2).

Abba Shaul says, a quarter- log is the initial [quantity of] blood of a child. The blood of a child, all of which flowed out and there is not a quarter- log : Rabbi Akiva says, [it is impure in] any amount, and the Sages say, [there must be] a quarter- log (Mishnah Oholot 2:2). For Rabbi Akiva says, impurity is in the blood and impurity is in the bones. Just as bones are impure even if they are less than a quarter-kav, so too blood is impure even if it is less than a quarter- log . They came back to Rabbi Akiva with three responses. "No. If you hold that as to bones, where the majority [of the bones of the body] are impure even if they are less than a quarter-kav, could you say the same regarding blood, which is only impure if there is a quarter- log ?" Another matter: "No. If you hold that as to bones, where even a minority of bones can be impure [if they comprise the majority of the skeletal structure], and [even] a bone the size of a barleycorn that separates from them is impure, could you say the same regarding blood, which is only impure if there is a quarter- log ?" Another matter: "No. If you hold that as to bones, where it is known that all of them are in front of you, could you say the same regarding blood? For we say that if even the smallest drop is left over, it is pure." He said to them, "Even I only hold such in a situation where all of it came out." They said to him, "That is impossible."

A quarter-kav of bones from the majority of the skeleton in size, and bones of (i.e., comprising) the majority of the skeleton in size, even though they do not contain a quarter-kav, are impure. A quarter-kav of bones from the majority of the skeleton in quantity, and bones of the majority of the skeleton in quantity, even though they do not contain a quarter-kav, are impure. Rabbi Yehuda stated a different version [of the foregoing halacha]: Beit Shammai say, a quarter-kav of bones from the skeleton from the structural majority or from numerical majority, [or] the structural majority or numerical majority of a corpse (i.e., considering the limbs as opposed to the bones), even though they do not contain a quarter-kav, are impure. And what is its "structural [majority]"? The calves and the thighs, and the ribs, and the spinal column. And what is its "numerical [majority]"? The digits of its hands and its feet, as long as they comprise [one hundred] twenty-five. * Said Rabbi Yehoshua, I can reconcile the words of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel [as follows]: One from the calves and from the thighs. It comes out to be the structural majority in size; and half of the numerical majority, and half of the structural majority do not join together [for purposes of impurity]. The equivalent of half of an olive's-bulk of flesh and half of an olive's-bulk of decomposed corpse matter do join with one another, and the remainder of all the impurities from a corpse do not join with one another, because their measurements are not equivalent.

The tombstone (i.e. a large stone laid horizontally over a grave, akin to a roof) and the stone frame supporting the tombstone defile by touch and by a tent, but they do not defile by carrying. Rabbi Eliezer says, they defile by carrying, from a logical deduction ( kal v'chomer ), for if they defile by touch, which is light, should they not defile [by carrying], which is stringent? Rabbi Akiva said to him, "If they defile by touch, which is more common, should they defile by carrying, which is less common?" Rabbi Eliezer said to him, "What is this, Akiva? For isn't it true that tent-impurity is less common than both of them, yet behold, they defile in it. And if they defile in a tent, which is less common, should they not defile by carrying, which is more common?" Rabbi Akiva was dismissed. Then Rabbi Yehoshua jumped up. He said to him, "Tent-impurity is more common than carrying-impurity, for one who tents over a corpse with a sukkah is impure, while one who moves it is pure." Said Rabbi Shimon, this is how it is judged: If there is a sukkah with an entryway, behold, it interposes on top of [the corpse], and if there is a sukkah without an entryway, that is itself a "tombstone." Rather, this is how it one should consider it: Tent-impurity is more common than carrying-impurity, for everything is defiled in a tent, and only a person is defiled by carrying. § It so happened in Beit Dagan in Judea that there was someone who died on the evening before Passover, and they went to bury him and the women * entered and they tied the rope to the tombstone. Then the men pulled from outside [and lowered the body into the grave] and the women entered to bury him, and then the men left and made their Pesach offerings in the evening [in a state of purity].

Two large stones of four by four handbreadths each that were made into a tombstone: One who tents over both of them is impure. [If] he removed one of them, one who tents over the second one is pure, because that impurity has a means of escape (see Mishnah Oholot 3:6).

Rabbi Yosei says, a ladleful of corpse-mold defiles by touch and by carrying and by tenting. Rabbi Shimon says, three impurities spread out from a corpse, each one of which defiles in two [ways] and does not [defile] in the third [way]. And they are: The tombstone, and the frame supporting the tombstone, and a bone the size of a barleycorn, [and] a ladleful of corpse-mold. The tombstone and the frame supporting the tombstone defile by touch and by airspace (=tenting), but they do not defile by carrying. And where [is impurity imparted] by carrying? By a bone the size of a barleycorn. A bone the size of a barleycorn defiles by touch and by carrying * , but it does not defile by tenting. And where [is impurity imparted] by tenting? By a ladleful of corpse-mold. A ladleful of corpse-mold defiles by carrying and by tenting, but it does not defile by touch. And so too would Rabbi Yosei say, an olive's-bulk from a corpse that was divided even into ten [pieces] defiles by carrying and by tenting, but does not defile by touch.

Said Rabbi Yehuda: There were six things that Rabbi Akiva had rendered impure but then changed his mind about. It so happened that they brought boxes of bones from K'far Tavi, and they they set them down in the open-air [courtyard] of the synagogue of Lod. And Theodoros the Physician entered, and all the other physicians with him, and they said, "There is neither a spine of a corpse or a skull of a corpse here." They said, "Since there are those that render [such incomplete corpses] impure and there are those that render them pure, we will stand up and take a vote." They started from Rabbi Akiva and he declared them pure. They said to him, "Since you had rendered pure what you had [previously] rendered impure, they will be pure." Said Rabbi Shimon, "[Rather,] until the day of Rabbi Akiva's death, he rendered it impure, and if he changed his mind after his death, I haven't heard of it."

The fat of a corpse that was complete and they cut it up is impure. [If] it was scattered around and they melted it * , it is pure, for that which is joined by human [agency] is not [considered] joined [for purposes of impurity]. An etrog that burst open, and they stuck it [back together] with a reed or a splinter of wood is not [considered] joined, for that which is joined by human [agency] is not [considered] joined. A marrow-bone of a corpse that was fashioned into the handle of a knife, behold, that is not [considered] joining by human [agency]. [If] one joined an olive's bulk of a corpse that had split into two, it is impure, and one need not be concerned lest it is deficient. An etrog that was cut into two is pure, and one need not be concerned lest it is deficient. A grain-offering that was mixed by five priests is fit [for the Altar], and one need not be concerned lest it is deficient. [If] it was transferred from vessel to vessel it [remains] fit. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, if he apportioned it [among the priests], behold, it is disqualified. The equivalent of an olive's bulk from a corpse, and the equivalent of an olive's bulk of decayed matter, a ladleful of corpse-mold from two corpses join together with one another. A ladleful of corpse-mold: Whenever there is even a small amount of dirt in it, it is impure, and Rabbi Yehoshua renders it pure because it was neutralized.

A quarter- log of blood that was absorbed into clothing -- how is it measured? One brings a large amount of water and launders [the clothing] in it, and brings another [container of] water and pours a quarter- log of blood into it. If they look the same (i.e., the shade of red is the same), behold, it is impure, and if not, it is pure. Rabbi Yosei says, the earlier Elders say, from the downward slope and within, the house is impure, and from the downward slope and outward, the house is pure (see Mishnah Oholot 3:3). They came back and said, as to a slope, whether it is from the inside or from the outside, the house is pure. [If] the corpse is outside and his hair is inside, even though there is only the smallest amount under the tent, the house and one who overtents it is impure.
All fluids from a corpse are pure except for its blood. And all who see the blood of a corpse, behold, they are impure.

And what is "mixed blood" (see Mishnah Oholot 3:5)? Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda says, one who was killed, from whom a quarter- log of blood came out in his life and in his death (i.e., while he was still alive and after his death). There is a doubt if it came out in his life, and there is a doubt if it came out in his death, and there is a doubt if [it came out both] in his life and in his death -- that is "mixed blood." And the Sages say, [if] the doubt occurred in a private domain, it is impure; in a public domain, it is pure. Rather, what is "mixed blood"? One who was killed, from whom a quarter- log of blood in his life and in his death, and it still did not cease [flowing], there is doubt if the majority [came out] in his life and the minority in his death, and a doubt if the majority [came out] in his life and the majority in his death -- behold, that is "mixed blood." Rabbi Yehuda says, one who was killed, who was moved onto a bed, and his blood drips out into a hole -- it is impure, because the drop of death is mixed in with it. And the Sages render it pure, because each first [drop] and every other first [drop] is separated [from the other drops; thus, every new drop is nullified] (see Nidd. 71b:1). Rabbi Shimon says, one who is crucified whose blood streams out, and a quarter- log of blood is found under him -- it is impure. And Rabbi Yehuda renders it pure, for I could say that the last drop had been "standing" on the wood [of the cross] * . In that way, it comes out that you can say, there are three quarter- logs . How so? He received a death-blow, and he was quivering, and a quarter- log of blood came out from him. And they uprooted him [from where he was lying] under the presumption that he was alive, and moved him to another place, and a quarter- log of blood came out from him. [And afterwards they found him dead, and a quarter- log came out of him (GR"A).] The first is the blood of life, the second is the mixed blood, and the third is the blood of death. * And what is the [practical] difference between the blood of death and the mixed blood? Rather, that [in regards to the blood of death] the nazir must shave on account of [touching it]; and they are liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects; [while in regards to] mixed blood, the nazir does not shave on account of it, and they are not liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects.

Said Rabbi Elazar: Originally, the Elders were divided. Some said, a quarter- log of blood, a quarter-kav of bones, and others said, a half-kav of bones and a half- log of blood. The Beit Din that came after them said, a quarter- log of blood [and] a quarter-kav of bones for terumah and sacrifices, [and] a half-kav of bones and a half- log of blood for the nazir and the Temple. Said Rabbi Elazar: When I went to Damascus, I found Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda ben P'tirosh * , who were sitting and deliberating about halacha. Yehuda ben P'tirosh says, "A nazir does not shave on account of a quarter- log of blood, and they are not liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects." Rabbi Meir said to him, "Let this be logically derived from a sheretz. Just as a nazir shaves on account of a sheretz, which is a light matter, and they are liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects, does it not logically follow that in regards to a quarter- log of blood, which is stringent, a nazir should shave on account of it, and they should be liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects?" Yehuda ben P'tirosh was silent. I said to Rabbi Meir, "Do not hold me in contempt [for saying this]. Are you familiar with Yehoshua ben Mamal?" He said to me, "Yes, and he was a master of m'lachot * ." I said to him, "In the following way did he (i.e., Yehoshua ben Mamal) speak to me in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: 'Every [form of] impurity from a corpse on account of which the nazir shaves, they are liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects, and every [form of] impurity from a corpse on account of which the nazir does not shave, they are not liable on its account for impurity to the Temple and its consecrated objects.'"

Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei says in the name of Rabbi Natan: [In regards to] a tent that is less than four handbreadths, its opening [for purposes of permitting impurity to escape] is its full width and its roof is pure. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir, a corpse that is more than four handbreadths, [the requisite size of its] opening is the entire open space. Rabbi Yosei says, the spinal column and the skull are the equivalent of a corpse [for purposes of impurity]. Others say in the name of Rabbi Natan, all the impurities that spread out from a corpse are like a corpse, and its opening is four handbreadths.

A drainpipe that is arched under the house (הבית): If it is four handbreadths wide and has an outlet four handbreadths wide, and [there is] a miscarried fetus inside it, the house remains pure. [If there is] a miscarried fetus in the house, whatever is inside [the drainpipe] remains pure. [If] it has a width of four handbreadths, but its outlet is less than four handbreadths, [and there is] a miscarried fetus inside it, the house is impure. [If there is] a miscarried fetus in the house, whatever is inside [the drainpipe] remains pure. [If] it is less than four handbreadths wide and its outlet is less than four handbreadths wide, [and there is] a miscarried fetus inside it, the house is impure. [If there is] a miscarried fetus inside the house, whatever is inside [the drainpipe] is impure. [If] it is wide from within but narrow from without, [and] the impurity is in the wide part, the house is impure. [If] in the narrow part, it is adjudged half and half. [If] it is impure, whether in the wide part or whether in the narrow part of the house, it is impure inside the house. * Vessels that are in the wide part are pure, and those that are in the narrow part are impure. Rabbi Yehuda agrees that with regards to crags and crevices, that although they are not similar to a tent, yet they are considered to be [halachically] like a tent (see Mishnah Oholot 3:7).

A cupboard standing either in the house or in the open air: [If] the impurity is inside it, vessels within its thickness (i.e., within niches in the walls of the cupboard) are pure. Impurity that is in its thickness: Vessels that are within (i.e., within the main body of the cupboard but not within the thickness) are pure. And Rabbi Yosei says, it is divided half and half. [If] it was standing inside the house, and the impurity was inside it, the house is impure. [If] the impurity was in the house, whatever is inside [the cupboard] is pure, for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. Vessels that are [lodged] between it and the ground, or that are between it and the wall [of the house], or that are between it and the roof-beam: If there exists there an opening of one handbreadth, they are impure, and if not, they are pure. [If] the impurity is there * , the house is impure. That which is within the wall and outward, and that which is in the plasterwork [in the ceiling] and above is adjudged [by the rule of] half and half.

Impurity under [the cupboard's] leg or on top of its leg, and [the cupboard] is tightly packed * , the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. To what is this similar? To a column that stands inside the house, and impurity is beneath it, and it is tightly packed (i.e., flush with the floor), the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. [If] he was transporting it on its side and it is closed, and the impurity is under it, opposite its thickness, or on top of its doors, and it is tightly packed, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. Vessels that are in niches of partition walls, on this side or on that side, are pure.

[If the cupboard] was standing inside the entrance [of the house] and opened up toward the outside, [and] the impurity is inside it, the house is pure. [If] the impurity [is in the house], that which is inside [the cupboard] is pure, for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. Said Rabbi Yosei, this is indeed the halacha. When is the power to save (i.e., to prevent impurity from spreading) greater than the power of a tightly fitting lid or the power of tents? If it saves, it [also] has the power of a tightly fitting lid in regards to a tombstone, and by a fortiori reasoning, on account of tenting.

[If the cupboard's] wheel-base protruded behind it three fingerbreadths, and impurity is there (i.e., in the wheel-base) under the roof-beams, the house is impure * , for I can view the roof-beams as though they descend [to up floor] and are stopped up. Another version: Impurity does not enter into a tent and only exits from it through an opening [the width] of a handbreadth. § Vessels that are opposite the corner [of two adjoining walls]: Rebbi renders them impure and the Sages render them pure. Said Rebbi, "I prefer their words to my words." When do these words apply? With regard to one that is burst open, but with regard to one that is stopped up, behold, it is like a sealed grave, and it is defiled by everything that is around it.

Said Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri came to the place of Rabbi Chalafta. He said to him, "What is your opinion about the eye of an oven?" He said to him, "It is impure." He said to him, "Even I say that, but Akiva holds that it's pure." The eye of an oven that is higher than a handbreadth but is not wider than a handbreadth, or which is not higher than a handbreadth, is pure. [If] he placed a board on top of a cleft, it is impure. The board is defiled and it defiles the oven.

An aruvah * between [the lower floor of] the house and the attic, and a cooking pot is placed on it, and it is punctured to allow liquids to enter: Rabbi Akiva says it saves (i.e., prevents the impurity in the lower floor from spreading to the attic, and the Sages say, it does not save. If it was opened such that olives could come out [through the puncture-hole], it saves up until an opening of a handbreadth. *

[A reed tube that was cut to hold waters of purification (Kel. 17:17), * ], and he poured waters of purification and ashes of purification inside of it: It saves on account of the purification [mixture] but it does not save on account of terumah; thus, it comes out that you could say, "The pure saves itself." How so? If there were [two vessels, one which was pure for purification, and one which was pure for terumah (GR"A)], it comes out that the vessel that was pure for purification saves itself, and the vessel that was pure for terumah saves itself.

A flask that [was defiled by corpse-impurity (Mishnah Oholot 5:4) and] is full of pure liquid, and one poured it out into another flask: If [the second flask] had liquid inside of it, it is impure * . A woman who was kneading in a kneading-trough, and her hands were [constantly] occupied with another dough, as long as she lifts up this one and sets down that one, [or] lifts up that one and sets down this one, the woman and the kneading-trough are impure with seven-day impurity, and the dough is pure. [If] she removed her hands from it and [then] returned them, she is defiled and she defiles the dough. Said Rabbi Yehoshua: "We were ashamed * by your words, Beit Shammai. Could it be possible for the woman and the kneading-trough to be impure with seven-day impurity, while the dough is pure? [Similarly, in the case of the flask, if] she removed her hands from it and [then] returned them, and defiled the flask * , should they be impure with seven-day impurity, while the liquid is pure?" After he had stood up, one student from among the students of Beit Shammai said before him, "Rabbi, may I speak before you the reason that Beit Shammai hold this way?" He said to him, "Speak." He said to him, "Vessels of amei ha'aratz * , what is their [presumptive] status, impure or pure?" He said to him, "Impure." "And if it is impure, does it save? If so, [the vessel of the am ha'aretz] will save with those of a chaver * ." Another version: "And what would an am ha'aretz say about his vessel, that it is impure? [Rather,] once we have rendered pure the food and drink inside it, we have rendered [the vessel] itself pure. But once you have rendered the vessel pure [ab initio], you have rendered both yours and his pure." Rabbi Yehoshua retracted and began teaching according to the words of that student. Said Rabbi Yehoshua, "I humble myself before you, bones of Beit Shammai."

Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, just as vessels save with respect to tents that have walls, so too they save with respect to tents that have no walls. Wooden vessels and earthenware vessels are both pure [and thereby save food, liquids, and other vessels within them (see Kel. 5:1)]. When do these words apply? With a vessel that has a handbreadth by a handbreadth [cavity] within it, but with a vessel that does not have a handbreadth by a handbreadth [cavity] within it, it does not save. When do these words apply? At a time that it is tightly sealed from the outside on one side, or from the inside on two sides; but if it was [only] tightly sealed equivalent to half a handbreadth on this side and equivalent to half a handbreadth on that side, behold, it does not save.

A cooking-pot that is placed on on the outer side of the wall of a tent, [and] the impurity is beneath it, and it is tightly packed, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. [If] it was one handbreadth higher than the ground, [and] the impurity is beneath it, [the area] beneath it is impure, [but the area] within it and above it is pure, because it saves along with the wall of the tent. [If the impurity] is inside it or above it, everything is impure.

[If] there was a large inverted basket [placed on the outer side of the wall of a tent (Mishnah Oholot 5:7)], and the impurity is beneath it, and it is tightly packed, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. . [If] it was one handbreadth higher than the ground, [and] the impurity is beneath it, [the area] beneath it is impure, [but the area] within it and above it is pure, because it is adjudged to be like the sloping parts of tents (see Mishnah Oholot 7:2). [If the impurity] is within it or on top of it, that which is directly above it, up to the firmament, is impure. [If the basket] was placed on top of two pegs from outside [the tent], pushed out from the opening [of the tent] by a handbreadth, it does not save. By less than a handbreadth: Rabbi Akiva says, it saves, and the Sages say, it does not save. A wall [separating a house from a garden], part of which serves the house, and part of which serves the garden, [and the basket] was placed on the side that serves the house, it saves the house [from impurity]; [but if it was placed on the side] that services the garden, it does not save.

A beam that is laid from one wall to another wall, and a cooking pot with it: If there is not an opening of a handbreadth between its mouth (i.e., of the cooking pot) and the beam, behold, it saves. If there is an opening of a handbreadth between its mouth and the beam, behold, it does not save. [If the cooking pot] was pressed tightly into the ground and onto the beam, if there is not an opening of a handbreadth between its mouth and the beam, behold, it saves. If there is an opening of a handbreadth between its mouth and the beam, it does not save. [If] its mouth was cleaved to the beam from above, behold, it saves; [but if] it was pushed away from it by an opening of a handbreadth, it does not not save. Less than a handbreadth: Rabbi Akiva says, it saves, and the Sages say, it does not save. Abba Shaul says, there was a dispute as to this. * [If] one end [of the beam] was placed onto the wall of a house, and one end was placed onto the wall of a garden, [if the cooking pot] was on the side that serves the house, it saves; on the side that serves the garden, it does not save. Abba Shaul says, even as to this, there was a dispute.

Four who were carrying a frame (i.e., which is being carried to a building ground, with tools and vessels above and below (Jastrow)), and its poles did not have the thickness of a yoke, [and] the impurity is beneath it, vessels that are on top of it are impure. [If] the impurity is above it, vessels that are beneath it are impure. Rabbi Eliezer renders them pure. And so too would Rabbi Eliezer say, [if there was] an olive's bulk from a corpse in the mouth of a raven (see Toh. 4:4), which tents over (i.e., flies directly above) the frame, the person and the vessels that are under it are pure; if it tents over an oven or a portable stove, they are pure. [If the frame] was set down on top of four vessels, even vessels of dung, or vessels of stone, or vessels of earth, and they do not have an opening of a handbreadth, [and] the impurity is beneath it, the vessels that are on top of it are impure. [If] the impurity is above it, vessels that are beneath it are impure. [If] they have an opening of a handbreadth, Rabbi Eliezer renders them pure, and if there is impurity beneath them, the vessels that are on top of it are impure. [In regards to] impurity that is above it, vessels that are beneath it are impure. [If] it was set down on four small bags, which [themselves] are placed on four stones, and they do not have the height of a handbreadth, [and] the impurity is beneath it, the vessels that are on top of it are impure. [If] the impurity is on top of it, vessels that are beneath it are impure, and Rabbi Eliezer renders them pure. If they have the height of a handbreadth, [and] the impurity is below it, they are impure, and Rabbi Eliezer renders them pure. If they have the height of a handbreadth, [and] the impurity is beneath it, vessels that are beneath it are pure, and if the tops of the small bags can be seen, [then] in either case, they are pure.

A plank, one ends of which was set down on top of a stone, and the other end of which was set down on top of a bench: The plank is viewed as if the bench was removed. [If] it could stand by itself [without the bench], it saves, and if not, it does not save. Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says, the plank is viewed as if it is lowered and sat down, and there is [still] a quarter of a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth height, behold, it saves because it is adjudged like the sloping sides of a tent. § Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, even if the door was left open, the house is pure, for the key was not defiled (see Mishnah Oholot 6:2).

A house that was partitioned off with pure wine jars and their mouths are nearer to the [area that is] pure, [the jars] save; [if they are] nearer to the [area that is] impure, they do not save. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon, [even if they are] nearer to the impure, they save, unless their mouths have an opening of a handbreadth. [If the jars] are plastered over with clay, whether from the inside or from the outside, if the plasterwork is capable of standing on its own, it saves, and if not, it does not save.

A wall that is cracked, whether vertically or horizontally, and it was made like a type of funnel -- wide on the inside (i.e., the side facing the house) and narrow on the outside -- [and] impurity is in the wide [side of the crack], the house is impure, and [if the impurity] is in the narrow [side], it is adjudged half and half (i.e., as though it were divided into separate halves (see Mishnah Oholot 6:3)). [If] the wide [side] is on the outside and the narrow [side] is on the inside, [and] impurity is in the wide [side], the house is pure, [and if the impurity] is in the narrow [side], it is adjudged half and half. [If] it was cracked vertically such that [the wall] was divided from top to bottom, [and] the wide [side of the crack] was on the top, and the narrow [side] was on the bottom, and the impurity was between the wide and narrow [sides], the house is impure; and [if] on the wide [side], the house is impure, and [if] on the narrow [side] it is adjudged half and half. And how big must this crack be? Rebbi says, the size of the fist of Ben Bati (a.k.a. "Ben Batiach," Kel. 17:12). A wall, half of which is rock and half of which is built [by man], it is adjudged half and half. [If] one removes [part of the wall] from the inside and [then] adds to it [on the outside (MS Vienna)], [ * and impurity is found in the inside half of the wall], the house is impure. [If] one removes [part of the wall] from the outside and [then] adds to it on the inside, and the impurity is found on the outside half of the wall, the house is pure.

[If] there was one of rock and one built [by man], that which is built is adjudged half and half, and that of rock is adjudged like a garlic-skin (see Mishnah Oholot 6:5 * ). Rabbi Yosei says, [if] the impurity is from the outer half of the wall, or from the upper half of the plasterwork [separating the main part of the house from the attic], the house is pure. One who stands directly above the impurity is is pure, for the impurity does not pass through the walls, and [that is true] even if there are no walls in the same direction. [In regards to a source of] impurity that is placed on top of a wall, whether on the inner half or the outer half, the house is pure. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon say, [if it is placed] on the outer half, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends.

A wall that is between two houses, and impurity is inside it: The house that is closer to the impurity is impure, and that which is closer to the purity (i.e., the side of the wall that is pure) is pure. Half and half, both of them are impure. Rabbi Eliezer says, they must burn their terumah [in both houses] on their account, but they are not liable on their account in regards to defilement of the Temple and its consecrated objects.

Plasterwork that is facing the open air * , and impurity is within it: [If the impurity is in] the lower half, the house is impure, and one who stands directly above the impurity is pure. [If the impurity is in] the upper half, [the house is pure,] and one who stands directly above the impurity is impure. Half and half, the house is impure, and one who stands directly below the impurity -- Rabbi Meir renders him impure and Rabbi Shimon renders him pure. Rabbi Yehuda says, every plasterwork services the house, and so too would Rabbi Yehuda say, every plasterwork services the attic. The Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda in the case of two caves, this one on top of that one, and the impurity is in the lower one, the lower one and the earth [under it] are impure, [and] the upper one and the earth [under it] are pure. [If] the impurity is in the upper one, the earth and the upper one are impure, [and] the earth and the lower one are pure, and the roof of the upper one is pure. And so too would Rabbi Yehuda say, [if there was] a wall between two burial niches, or between two caves, [and the wall was] less than six handbreadths [thick], it is adjudged half and half; more than that, it is adjudged like a garlic-skin (Mishnah Oholot 6:6).

A cooking pot that is placed on the side of the wall of a cave does not save. On the the arched entrance of the cave, behold, it does save. [If] it was placed in the window that is between two houses (i.e., which share a common wall), and impurity is in one of them, behold, it is pure because it is saved along with the walls of the second [house]. [If] there was impurity between them, and in its place (i.e., the window where the cooking pot sits) there is [the space of] a cubic handbreadth: If there is not the space of a handbreadth between the mouth of the cooking pot and the lintel, behold, it saves. [If] there is the space of a handbreadth between the mouth of the cooking pot and the lintel, it does not save.

The general rule of [the waters of] purification that are placed in the window, and in its place (i.e., of the source of impurity) there is [a space of] a cubic handbreadth: If there is not the space of a handbreadth between the mouth [of the vessel containing the waters of purification] and the lintel, behold, it saves, and if not, it does not save, the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And Rabbi Yehoshua says, it never saves unless in front of it there is an empty space of a handbreadth.

A column that is standing inside the house, and impurity is beneath it, and it is tightly packed, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends. And if in the place of impurity there is [a space of] a cubic handbreadth, behold, it is like a sealed grave, and it defiles all that is around it. Vessels that are under the "flower" (i.e., the piece that protrudes at the top of a column) are pure (Mishnah Oholot 6:7), and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri renders them impure.

A chest that was converted into a wall-closet (i.e., stood upright and affixed to the wall): Even though it serves [the wall], it is pure. [If] it was impure and converted into a wall-closet, it remains impure until it is affixed with a nail. A wall-closet that opens toward the house: [If] it is shut and impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, whatever is inside of it is pure, because the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. [If there is] impurity in the ground [under it] or in the wall that is before it, the impurity breaks through and ascends, breaks through and descends, and we view the wall-closet as though it is plugged up, [and it is adjudged] half-and-half to bring impurity into the house (Mishnah Oholot 6:7). Three wall-closets, one next to the other, or one behind the other, or one on top of the other, and impurity is beneath them, between them, or above them, the impurity breaks through and ascends, breaks through and descends, and we view the wall-closets as though they are plugged up, and they are are adjudged half-and-half to bring impurity into the house. [In connection with solid tomb monuments (Mishnah Oholot 7:1)] Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, one may support pure sukkot (booths) on them for the purpose of eating the Pesach offering in them.

[If] an olive's bulk of a corpse is on the rudad (i.e., the excess portion of the tent canvas that lays flat on the ground, forming the floor of the tent) * , or on top of [the tent], the impurity breaks through and ascends, breaks through and descends. [If] impurity is inside [the sloping part of the tent], one who touches it from within contracts seven-day impurity; [one who touches it] from the outside contracts evening-impurity. [If] impurity is outside it, one who touches it from the outside contracts seven-day impurity, and from within, evening-impurity, and one who enters [the tent without touching the sides of the tent] is pure. Half an olive's bulk inside and half an olive's bulk outside, one who touches it, either from the inside or from the outside, contracts evening-impurity, and the tent itself is impure with seven-day impurity. Said Rabbi Natan, one who saves through the agency of others, by a fortiori logic, [saves through] his own [agency].

A tent that was stretched out on top of four metal stakes: Rabbi Yaakov says, it does not save, because it is held up by something impure; and Rabbi Yosei says, it does save. [If it was] stretched out on top of forked reeds (see Sukkah 13a:4-5): Rabbi Yosei says, it saves, and Rabbi Shimon says, it does not save unless it is stretched out like a tent is [normally] stretched out.

A sheet that they sewed up and placed on top of a cradle: If there is not an opening of a handbreadth between it and the ground, behold, it saves. When do these words apply? In a situation where if you removed the cradle, the sheet would remain standing, but if you remove the cradle and the sheet falls, even though it is sewn up and even though it was raised from the ground even the smallest amount, behold, it does not save. And if it was the mat of a tent, even if it was not sewn up, and he did not intend it, and there is not the opening of a handbreadth between it and the ground, behold, it saves. And if there is between it and the ground the opening of a handbreadth, it does not save.

[If] the corpse is in the house, and it has many entrances, all of which are locked, all of them are impure. [If] one of them is opened, even though he did not intend for it [to serve as the exit for the impurity], all of them are purified. [If] there were many windows in it, and all of them were blocked, all of them are pure. [If] they were opened, all of them are impure, and they do not save on behalf of the entrances. [If there was] a small entrance within a large entrance, that which forms a tent on top of both of them is impure. [If] he intended to bring out [the corpse] through the small [entrance], the small one purifies the large one. [If] there were two [entrances] running alongside each other, that which forms a tent on top of both of them is impure. [If] he intended to bring out [the corpse] through one of them, behold, its fellow is pure. [If] it had one entrance facing north and one entrance facing south, and he intended to bring out [the corpse] through its northern [entrance], [and] afterwards his brothers or relatives came and said, "We can only bring him out through its southern [entrance]," the southern has purified the northern, as long as as they do not employ artifice. And if they employed artifice, behold, they (i.e., the entrances) are impure.

Houses that open up into a portico, and the corpse is in one of them: If the normal way for the corpse to be taken out is through the courtyard, the gatehouse and the [other] houses are pure. If not, the gatehouse is impure and the [other] houses are pure. If there was a closed room with the house, and the impurity (i.e., the corpse) was brought inside of it through the window, that which is outside [the room] is pure, because impurity goes out in the same way it comes in. Rabbi Yehuda says, [in regards to] one who makes an opening for the first time, Beit Shammai say, [it protects the other entrances from defilement] once it is opened four handbreadths, and Beit Hillel say, once one begins to open it up (contra Mishnah Oholot 7:2). [If the entrance] was blocked up, Beit Shammai says, [it protects] once he begins [to remove the blockage], and Beit Hillel say, once he intends [to remove the blockage].

Stillborn infants are not subject to [the laws of] "the opening of the grave" (Mishnah Oholot 7:4) until their heads are rounded like the spindle-knob of the warp [of a loom], the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says, like the spindle-knob of the woof. Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Tzadok says, when t'fifiyot * have formed. Said Rabbi Yosei, I say one thing and they said one thing. I say to them that [regarding] the nature of impurity, its nature is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. And they said to me, a newborn does not possess impurity until it goes out into the air of the world.

Rabbi Eliezer (alt., "Rabbi Meir" (MS Vienna)) says, [if] a Nazir and a corpse were under the stomach of a camel (i.e., such that the camel forms a "tent" over them), the Nazir does not shave on its account * , and they are not liable on its account for defilement of the Temple and its consecrated objects.

Impurity that is placed in a wall, even half and half, and so too a herd of livestock, wild animals, and birds (see Mishnah Oholot 8:1), and so too living creatures * who walk single file, even if the head of this one is between the legs of that one, and the head of that one is between the legs of this one, the Nazir does not shave on their account, and they are not liable on their account for defilement of the Temple and its consecrated objects.

[If] one was pressed to work at a mill where there is an idolater or a menstruant, his clothes possess midras -impurity. What kind of a mill? Any that can (alt., "cannot" (Rash MiShanz)) be removed or pushed from its place. In the matter of corpse-impurity, his clothes are pure unless his clothes touch an opening of a handbreadth.

And what are "interlaced boughs" [that bring forth impurity and protect against it]? A tree which casts shade over the ground. Rabbi Yehuda says, we look at the lower ones as if they ascend to the top, and the upper ones as if they descend to the bottom, and if this one touches that one with an opening of a handbreadth, they bring forth impurity and protect against it. What are "protrusions"? A protrusion that projects out from a fence. * [If] they were placed on top of the fence, [Rabbi Yehuda says, * ] we look at them as if stones were pressed down on top of them. [If] they had rotted, we look at them as if they were metal stakes, and if they were thinned out [such that they became separated] from one another, if they could [nonetheless] support thin plasterwork, [they bring forth and protect against impurity], the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say, medium plasterwork. Rabbi Yehuda says, if you pull a thread from one side to the other side and it touches, even if they do not intend it, behold, that blocks * [the impurity].

Rabbi Yosei says, the ropes of a bed, and window-lattices protect [both] the house and the attic, unless the impurity crosses over to the other side. [If] they had placed [the ropes or the lattices] on top of a corpse in the open air, that which forms a tent opposite the perforation is impure, and that which is not opposite the perforation is pure, because impurity goes out in the same way that it entered. Rabbi Yehuda says, if they are [not] able to * support medium plasterwork, they do not protect. [If] they had placed [the ropes or the lattices] inside the house, behold, they protect, for I can look at the beams as if they descend and conceal [the empty space]. Rabbi Yosei says, [in regards to] a cupboard that is filled with vessels, and he threw it on top of an olive's-bulk of a corpse, they are impure, for if [the cupboard] was placed on top of a corpse in the open air, they would be pure.

A plank that is floating on the face of the water: [If] impurity is on the side, vessels that are on that side are pure. Rabbi Ya'akov says, we look at the plank as if it has descended and settled, and there is under it a handbreadth cubed. [If] impurity is on one side and vessels are on the other side, they are pure. Three houses, this one inside of that one, and half an olive's-bulk [of a corpse] in the inner one or in the middle one, and half an olive's-bulk in the outer one: The outer one is impure, [and] the inner one and the middle one are pure. [If] half an olive's-bulk is in the inner one or half an olive's-bulk is in the middle one, the inner one is pure, and the outer one and the middle one are impure. Said Rabbi Yehuda: I say one thing and they said one thing. I say to them, "Rabbi Eliezer concedes to Rabbi Yehoshua regarding two jars that are open inside a house, [that] it is impure. About what did they disagree? About two rooms of a house, for Rabbi Eliezer renders it impure, and Rabbi Yehoshua renders it pure." And they said to me, "Rabbi Yehoshua concedes to Rabbi Eliezer regarding two open rooms inside a house, that the house is pure. About what did they disagree? About two jars, for Rabbi Eliezer renders it impure and Rabbi Yehoshua renders it pure."

A k’veret (a large, hive-shaped grain receptacle) * that is inside a house, and a k'fisha (an inverted basket of twigs, not susceptible to impurity) is placed over its mouth: Rabbi Yehuda says, it saves [from impurity], and the Sages say, it does not save. For Rabbi Yehuda says, just as a plank saves, so too a k'fisha saves. [But if] it was laying down on its side with a handbreadth's opening [between the k'fisha and the k'veret ], all agree that it does not save.

A column [comprised] of cooking pots that is standing inside a house, from the ground until the roof-beams, [with] the bottom rim of this one on the mouth of that one, and the bottom rim of that one on the mouth of the next: If [between] the uppermost mouth and the roof-beams there is not at least a handbreadth's opening, and between the bottom rim of the bottommost one * and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside [the column], the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside [the column] is pure, for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature [is not] to enter. If there is at least a handbreadth's opening between the uppermost mouth and the roofbeams, and at least a handbreadth's opening between the bottom rim of the bottommost one and the ground, [and] impurity is inside [the column], the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside of [the column] is pure (alt., "impure" (GR"A)). [If] there was one [cooking pot] that was impure, and it was placed in the middle, and in its place there is [an empty space of] a handbreadth by a handbreadth by the height of a handbreadth, [and] impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside of it is impure. [If] in its place there is not [an empty space of] a handbreadth by a handbreadth by the height of a handbreadth, [and] impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is inside the house, that which is inside [the cooking pot] is pure.

A pittus (a large earthenware cask or tub) that is standing inside a house, from the ground until the roof beams: If between its mouth and the roof-beams there is not at least a handbreadth's opening, and between its bottom rim and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside of [the pittus ] is pure, for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. If between its mouth and the roof-beams there is at least a handbreadth's opening, and between its bottom rim and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside of [the pittus ] is impure. [If] it had a narrow mouth, and between its shoulder (i.e., the point at which the vessel widens) and the roof-beams there is not at least a handbreadth's opening, behold, it saves [from impurity], and if not, it does not save, unless there is a handbreadth's opening in its shoulder * . [If] its bottom rim was sharp, and there is not a handbreadth's opening between its bottom rim and the ground, behold, it saves, and if not, it does not save unless there is a handbreadth's opening in its bottom rim. [If] there was a damaged k'veret [whose holes were] stopped up with straw, even if it is a cubit above the ground, behold, it saves.

A [damaged] k'veret that is standing inside the entrance [and] blocks up the entire entrance: If between its mouth and the lintel there is not at least a handbreadth's opening, and between its bottom rim and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside of it, the house is pure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside of [the k'veret ] is pure (alt., "impure" (MS Vienna)), for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. If there is a handbreadth's opening between its mouth and the lintel, and impurity is inside of it, the house is impure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside [the k'veret ] is impure. If between its sides and the doorposts there is not (alt., "there is" (GR"A)) at least a handbreadth's opening, and between its bottom rim and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside [the k'veret ], the house is pure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside [the k'veret ] is pure.

Two k'verot that are standing inside the entrance and block up the entire entrance: [If] the bottom rim one is not on top of that of the other, [and] if between the upper one and the lintel there is not at least a handbreadth's opening, and between the mouth of the lower one and the ground at least a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is within it, the house is pure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is within [the k'veret ] is pure, for the nature of impurity is to go out, and its nature is not to enter. [If] between the mouth of the upper one and the lintel there is a handbreadth's opening, and between the mouth of the bottom one and the earth there is a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside it, the house is impurity. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside [the k'veret ] is impure. The vessels that are between them are pure. If between their sides and the doorposts there is a handbreadth's opening, and between them and the ground a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is inside them, the house is pure. [If] impurity is in the house, that which is inside [the k'veret ] is pure. [If] one of them was defiled, it is impure, and the house and its fellow [ k'veret ] are pure, and so too the mouth of this one on top of the bottom rim of that one, and so too the bottom rim of this one on top of the bottom rim of that one. And what is "loosely placed" (Mishnah Oholot 9:3)? Anything that has a handbreadth's opening in all four directions, or from three directions, or from two directions, one opposite the other. What is "stuck" (Mishnah Oholot 9:7)? Anything that does not have handbreadth's [opening] from [even] one direction. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon agree that in regards to impurity under the stoppage, the impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends.

[If] it was sitting on its bottom rim in the open air, [and] impurity is inside it, that which touches it anywhere is impure * , the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say, it is only impure opposite its covering. [But] if it was overturned onto its mouth, that which touches it anywhere is impure.

A burial vault (lit., a "coffin") that was carved out from a large rock and covered [with a gravestone], that which touches [the stone] anywhere is pure, and only [the burial vault's] mouth is impure, for there is no impurity except for that which is opposite its cavity. [If] it was built with the wall of a tomb-structure: If even the smallest amount of [the impurity] was visible inside the tomb-structure, one who enters inside of it is impure, and if not, it is only impure opposite its covering. [If] one built a tomb-structure on top of it, behold, it is like a sealed grave, and it defiles all its surroundings. [If] it was made like a type of sarcophagus, that which touches it anywhere is pure. If it was the same [width above and below (Mishnah Oholot 9:15)]: Rabbi Eliezer renders it impure, and Rabbi Yehoshua says, from a handbreadth and above, it is impure, from a handbreadth and below it is pure, for [by way of analogy,] burnt offerings are not raised higher than a handbreadth from the ground (cf. Zevachim 58a:10).

[If] a cask is sitting on its bottom rim in the open air, and an olive's-bulk from a corpse is placed under its bottom rim, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends, and the cask is impure. [If] part of an olive's-bulk from a corpse is placed under [the cask's rounded] sides and part of it is placed under its bottom rim, whatever is opposite the impurity, whether above or below, is impure, and whatever is not opposite the impurity, whether above or below, is pure. And if within its sides there is a handbreadth's opening, everything is impure * . Two half olive-bulks, one placed under the [cask's rounded] sides and one placed under its bottom rim, whatever is opposite the impurity, whether above or below, is impure, and whatever is not opposite opposite the impurity, whether above or below, is pure.

A cooking pot that is placed on the side of the threshold [of a house] such that if it was raised and its rims were protruding from the lintel by even the smallest amount, the impurity breaks out and ascends, breaks out and descends.

[If the cooking pot] was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, and impurity was under it, inside it, or on top of it, everything is impure, and the house is pure. [If the impurity is] in the house, only the house is impure. Should it be elevated and its wall (i.e., the rounded side of the cooking pot) touches * the lintel by less than an opening of a handbreadth by even the smallest amount, * and impurity is under it, and it is tightly packed, the impurity breaks through and ascends, [and] breaks through and descends.

[If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, and impurity was under it, inside it, or above it, the house is pure because it saved along with the "walls of a tent." Inside it or on top of it, everything is impure, and the house is pure. [If the impurity is] in the house, only the house is impure. [If it was placed] such that if it were raised and its wall would touch the lintel over a [space of] a handbreadth's opening, [and] impurity is under it, and it is tightly packed, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends.

[If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, [and] impurity was under it or in the house, [the space] below it and the house are impure, [but the space] inside it or above it are pure (i.e., the same as with a k'veret (Mishnah Oholot 9:4)). [If impurity is] inside it or on top of it, everything is impure. [If it was placed] such that if it were raised and its rims [were to] cover up (lit., "its lips [were to] eat") the lintel in even the smallest amount, [and] impurity is inside of it, and it is tightly packed, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends. [If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, if [the cooking pot's] wall has a handbreadth's opening [within it] and impurity is under it, or in the house, inside it, or on top of it, everything is impure. [If] its wall does not have a handbreadth's opening [within it], [and] impurity is under it, [the space] under it is impure, and [the space] inside of it * and on top of it and the house are pure, because it saves along with the "walls of a tent." Inside of it or on top of it, everything is impure, and the house is pure, because it saves along with the "walls of a tent." Inside of it or on top of it, everything is impure and the house is pure. In the house, only the house is impure.

[If] it was placed under the aperture [of a roof], such that if it were raised and its rims were to touch the roof in any amount, [and] impurity is under it, and it is tightly packed, [then] impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends. [If] it was raised above the ground a handbreadth and impurity is under it, or in the house, or inside of it, or on top of it, everything is impure. [If it was placed] such that if it were raised upwards, and it sat in the aperture and closed up the [opening of the] entire aperture, and impurity is under it, and it is tightly packed, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends. [If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, [and] impurity is under it, or in the house under it, and the house is impure, [that which is] inside it or above it is pure. [If impurity is] inside it or directly above it, up until the firmament, [everything] is impure. [If it is placed] such that if it were raised upwards and it went into the aperture, [and] there is not at least a handbreadth's opening between it and the aperture, and impurity is [under it (MS Vienna)], and it is tightly packed, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends.

[If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth, and impurity is under it, [the area] under it is impure. Inside of it, and on top of it, and the house are pure because it is saved along with the walls of the tent. [If impurity is] inside of it or on top of it, everything is impure. [If it was placed] such that if it was raised upwards and goes up into the aperture, and there is between it and the aperture a handbreadth's opening, and impurity is under it, [and] it is tightly packed, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends.

[If] it was raised above the ground by a handbreadth [and] impurity is under it, [the area] under it is impure; inside it, and above it, and the house are pure because they are adjudged to be likened to the sloping walls of tents. [If impurity is] inside it or on top of it, everything is impure, and the house is pure. [If impurity is] in the house, only the house is impure.

An aperture that [opens up] to the [outside] air, and does not have (alt., "and has" (GR"A)) a handbreadth's opening, and an olive's-bulk of a corpse is placed under it, and he placed something that is susceptible to impurity [in the aperture]: If there is a handbreadth's opening there, everything is impure, and if not, it is not impure except that which is directly [above] the olive's-bulk of the corpse.

An aperture that [opens up] to the [outside] air and does not have a handbreadth's opening, and an olive's-bulk of a corpse is placed under it, the house is impure and the one who overtents it is impure, the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says, the one who overtents it is pure. Rabbi Shimon says, if the impurity was [in position] before his leg [passed over] the aperture, the house is impure, and the one who overtents it is impure, and if not, the house is impure and the one who overtents it is pure. [If] some of the impurity is in the house and some is directly below the aperture, the house is impure and the one who overtents it is impure, the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say, the one who overtents it is pure. Rabbi Yosei says, if this is not [the type] of impurity that can be divided, such as an olive's bulk of the spinal column or the skull of a corpse, the house is impure [and the one who overtents it is pure (MS Vienna; GR"A)], and if not, the house is pure and the one who overtents it is impure.

Two half olive's-bulks, [one] placed inside the house, and one placed directly [below] the aperture: The one who overtents [the aperture] is pure. [If] the one that was placed inside the house is pushed [such that it is] directly [below] the aperture, it is as though everything is directly [below] the aperture.

An olive-bulk of a corpse in the mouth of a raven, and one who erects a tent on top of the aperture [of a roof] whose width is less than a handbreadth: The house is impure. Rabbi Yosei renders it pure until there is impurity of a handbreadth's width across.

A vessel containing [the waters of] purification that is placed in the aperture: If it is lowered down [through the aperture], it is impure, and if it is not lowered down, it is pure. When do these words apply? In regards to an aperture that does not have an opening of a handbreadth, but in regards to to an aperture that has an opening of a handbreadth, whether it is lowered down or whether it is not lowered down, it is impure. When do these words apply? In regards to an earthenware [vessel], but as in regards to that of stone (alt., "wood" (GR"A)), whether or not it has an opening of a handbreadth, and whether or not it is lowered down, it is pure.

[An aperture] that is between the house and the attic, and there is not a handbreadth's opening in [the aperture], [and] impurity is in the house, vessels that are in the attic are pure. [If] impurity is in the attic, vessels that are in the house are pure, for I could view the roof-beams as though they descend and close off [the opening]. Another reason: Impurity can neither enter a tent nor leave a tent except through a handbreadth's opening. Vessels that are directly above the house: Rebbi renders them impure and the Sages render them pure. Said Rebbi, I prefer their words to my words.

[Two] apertures, this one on top of that one, and they have a handbreadth's opening, and something that is susceptible to impurity is placed [directly under them], if there is a handbreadth's opening, everything is impure, and if not, only that which is directly [below] the lower one is impure. [If] they are wide from the top and narrow from the bottom, from the narrow part * and below is impure; from the narrow part and above is pure. [If] they are wide from the bottom and narrow from the top, there is only impurity directly [below] the narrow part.

And how large must this split be [in a house such that each half is considered separate for purposes of corpse-impurity (Mishnah Oholot 11:1)]: Beit Hillel say, even the smallest amount, the [width of] the string of a plumb-line, and Rabbi Yosei says in the name of Beit Hillel, a handbreadth's opening. Said Rebbi: "I would be astonished if Rabbi Yosei said 'a handbreadth's opening' [in connection with a split house]. He only said that in regards to an olive's bulk of a corpse.” [If there is] impurity inside and vessels outside [the split], even though the crack is the smallest amount, the [width of] the string of a plumb-line, behold, that cuts off [the impurity from spreading].

An overturned seah-measure on top of an overturned [earthenware] jar, [or] two seating-blocks one on top of the other, and a stone on top of the [uppermost] seating-block, bring in impurity. A seah-measure sitting right-side-up, and a jar sitting right-side-up, an inflated water-skin, a cushion cover filled with straw * , a sheet cover filled with lumps of threads ( mochin ), a sheet cover filled with wrappings, two stones one on top of the other, and a seating block on top of the stone: [In all of these cases,] they do not bring in impurity.

A dog that consumed the flesh of a corpse and entered the house: The house is pure, for any matter that has been swallowed by a person, or by a domesticated animal, or by a wild animal, or by fowl, is clean. [If the dog] vomited them, the house is impure. [If the dog] died, if [the corpse matter] had stayed in its intestines for [less than] three full days while it was still alive, [the house is impure * ], and in regards to [corpse matter] in fowl and fish, immediately. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says, in regards to fish, immediately, and in regards to fowl, twenty-four hours. Rabbi Eliezer says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, in either case, twenty-four hours.

A cellar * and the candlestick * that is inside it, whose calyx protrudes, and an olive-basket * is placed over it [covering the mouth of the store-room (Mishnah Oholot 11:8)]: When do these words apply? When it is made of metal, but when it is made of wood, behold, it protects [the cellar from impurity even when the candlestick is removed]. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yosei says, when do these words apply? When it is made of wood, but when it is made of metal, it is defiled, and no impure vessel can protect [against impurity].

A wooden plank that is placed on the mouth of the cellar, and impurity is under it or on top of it, vessels that are directly above or below the overlap are impure (alt., "pure" (GR"A)). [If] there was an olive-basket, and it had a rim [that projected out] one handbreadth (i.e., to be used as a receptacle in its inverted state (Jastrow)), and impurity is under it, the vessels that are opposite the overlap, whether above or below, are impure. If [its rim] was flat, behold, it is like a wooden plank. Vessels that are directly above or below the overlap are impure (alt., "pure" (MS Vienna; GR"A)).

Walls of the house and walls of the cellar that were equal[ly wide] as one another, and impurity is either in the house or in the cellar, vessels that are in the walls of the house and that are in the walls of the cellar are adjudged half-and-half. But if the walls of the house are wider than those of the cellar, and impurity is inside the house, vessels that are in the walls of the cellar are impure, and those that are in the walls of the house are adjudged half-and-half. If the walls of the cellar were wider than those of the house, and impurity is in the house, vessels that are in the walls of the cellar are pure, [and] those that are in the walls of the house are adjudged half-and-half.
